templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation inside a compound joined by and
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Dash pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a past-participial phrase
items.passage: Monk parakeets are the only parrots known to construct nests out of sticks rather than nesting in tree cavities. Breeding pairs frequently build directly onto the nests of their ______ to by successive generations of birds over many years, these communal structures can eventually accommodate dozens of pairs, each with a separate entrance chamber.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Breeding pairs frequently build directly onto the nests of their neighbors” is a complete sentence. “Added to by successive generations of birds over many years” describes “these communal structures,” the subject of the next main clause (“these communal structures can eventually accommodate dozens of pairs ...”), so a period belongs after “neighbors.”

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “added to by successive generations ...” look like a modifier in the first clause, but “these communal structures can eventually accommodate ...” is a second main clause, so two main clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the phrase is glued to the first clause, and the comma before “these communal structures” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which are added to ...” turns the phrase into a relative clause in the first sentence, but the main clause “these communal structures can eventually accommodate ...” still follows with only a comma, so the sentence is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (bird behavior). Band 6: a 10-word past-participial opener that can hang on “neighbors” (or their nests) in A, B and D; the subject of clause 2 arrives 11 words after the blank (1b97cce9 “tombs. Built” menu, with “which are” as the added word). No semicolon or “, and” option. Facts kept general (the only stick-nesting parrot; shared nests with a separate entrance for each pair).

band7.why: As targeted: 10-word past-participle opener (“Added to by ...”) that can hang on “neighbors”; splice surfaces at “these communal structures” 11 words out; 1b97cce9 menu with “which are”.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a participial phrase that has internal commas
items.passage: In Edo-period Japan, merchant vessels known as kitamaebune sailed between Osaka and the northern island of Ezo (present-day Hokkaido), purchasing and reselling merchandise at ports along the ______ dried kelp, or kombu, from Ezo to markets farther south, these vessels helped establish the ingredient as a staple of Osaka’s cuisine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In Edo-period Japan, merchant vessels known as kitamaebune sailed between Osaka and the northern island of Ezo (present-day Hokkaido), purchasing and reselling merchandise at ports along the route” is a complete sentence. “Carrying dried kelp, or kombu, from Ezo to markets farther south” describes “these vessels,” the subject of the next main clause (“these vessels helped establish the ingredient ...”), so a period must follow “route.”

B.why_wrong: The comma lets “carrying dried kelp ...” read as a second modifier of the first clause, like “purchasing and reselling merchandise,” but “these vessels helped establish ...” is another main clause, so two main clauses are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “carrying dried kelp ...” attaches to the first clause, and the comma before “these vessels” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And carrying” pairs the phrase with “purchasing and reselling,” but the main clause “these vessels helped establish ...” still follows with only a comma, so the result is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (Edo-period coastal trade, Japan). Band 6: the 11-word opener carries its own commas (“dried kelp, or kombu,”) and reads as a second participle beside “purchasing and reselling” in B and C (886dc9f9 shape, “Bay and having” as the added-word option); clause 2’s subject comes 12 words after the blank. No semicolon or “, and” option (“, and carrying” would be correct). Facts kept general: the kitamaebune traded at each port on the Osaka to Ezo route and carried kombu south.

band7.why: As targeted: 11-word participial opener with its own commas reads as a second participle beside “purchasing and reselling”; 886dc9f9 menu (“and carrying”).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long past-participial phrase that could modify the last noun of the first
items.passage: Zimbabwean musician Thomas Mapfumo began performing in Shona in the 1970s, pioneering a distinctive form of popular ______ for electric guitar from the interlocking melodies of the mbira, a thumb piano central to Shona ceremonies, his style became known as chimurenga, a Shona word meaning “struggle.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Zimbabwean musician Thomas Mapfumo began performing in Shona in the 1970s, pioneering a distinctive form of popular music” is a complete sentence. “Adapted for electric guitar from the interlocking melodies of the mbira, a thumb piano central to Shona ceremonies” describes “his style,” the subject of the main clause that follows (“his style became known as chimurenga ...”), so a period belongs after “music.”

A.why_wrong: The phrase reads naturally as a description of “music,” but “his style became known as chimurenga” is a second main clause, so the comma alone joins two main clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the phrase becomes part of the first clause, and the comma before “his style” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “That was adapted ...” makes the phrase a relative clause describing “music” in the first sentence, but the main clause “his style became known as chimurenga ...” still follows with only a comma, producing a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music, Zimbabwe). Band 7 (band7/boundaries.md section 5, S1_period): an 18-word past-participial opener with an internal appositive that reads as a modifier of “music” (a872c60a “tenets. Developed by”, 0fa289a7); clause 2’s subject (“his style”) arrives 18 words after the blank, so the cue sits far outside a 6-word window; the run is 47 words. Facts kept to what is well known: Mapfumo sang in Shona, adapted mbira patterns to electric guitar, and the style is called chimurenga (Shona for struggle).

band7.why: 18-word past-participle opener with an inner appositive hangs naturally on “music”; the splice surfaces at “his style” 18 words after the blank; option set of a872c60a (comma, glued, “that was”).

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause; semicolon before it, comma after
items.passage: Japan’s furusato nozei (“hometown tax”) program, introduced in 2008, permits taxpayers to redirect a portion of their local taxes to any municipality they choose. Many participants do not contribute to the communities where they grew ______ they select municipalities offering the most attractive thank-you gifts, such as wagyu beef, crab, or rice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Many participants do not contribute to the communities where they grew up” and “they select municipalities offering the most attractive thank-you gifts ...” are both main clauses. A semicolon joins them, and “rather,” with its comma, opens the second clause, where it signals what participants do instead.

A.why_wrong: Commas around “rather” do not join two main clauses; “rather” is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark after “up,” the two main clauses run together; the comma after “rather” comes too late to separate them.

D.why_wrong: The semicolon after “rather” puts the adverb at the end of the first clause (“where they grew up, rather”), where it no longer introduces the alternative; “rather” belongs to the clause that tells what participants do instead.

items.notes: Subject: social science (public finance, Japan). Band 6: the a9e5b788 “; rather,” shape with the adverb placed on each side of the boundary; the band-7 adverb cell (w4b2_05) uses “though” closing clause 1 instead, so the two are not clones. Facts kept general (program introduced 2008; donors often choose municipalities for their gifts).

band7.why: As targeted: “; rather,” is a band 5 and 6 shape (a9e5b788); band 7 adverb items use “though”/“however” closing clause 1.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause (contrast with the previous sentence); semicolon after it
items.passage: Frogfish often remain motionless on reefs for hours, camouflaged so effectively that they resemble sponges or algae-encrusted rocks. Such stillness shouldn’t be mistaken for ______ when a fish or shrimp drifts within reach, a frogfish can expand its mouth and engulf the prey in a matter of milliseconds, far too rapidly for the victim to escape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Such stillness shouldn’t be mistaken for sluggishness, though” is a main clause, and “when a fish or shrimp drifts within reach, a frogfish can expand its mouth ...” is another. The semicolon after “though” joins them, and placing “though” in the first clause shows that this clause qualifies the previous sentence: frogfish stay motionless for hours, yet they are not slow.

A.why_wrong: Without a semicolon, “though” begins a subordinate clause (“though when a fish ... drifts within reach, a frogfish can expand its mouth ...”), which illogically presents the frogfish’s fast strike as contrary to the claim that its stillness isn’t sluggishness; the two ideas agree.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must be followed by a main clause, but “though when a fish ... a frogfish can expand its mouth ...” is a subordinate clause beginning with “though.”

D.why_wrong: Commas around “though” leave the main clauses “Such stillness shouldn’t be mistaken for sluggishness” and “a frogfish can expand its mouth ...” joined by commas alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (fish predation). Band 7 (band7/boundaries.md section 5, S1_adverb): “though” closes clause 1, which corrects the expectation set by the previous sentence (motionless for hours, yet not sluggish), and clause 2 elaborates it; A is wrong only by meaning (subordinate “though” would set the fast strike against “not sluggish”), B is the textbook placement that fails on grammar, D a splice. The deciding cue is in the previous sentence. Facts kept general (frogfish camouflage; a strike measured in milliseconds).

band7.why: “though” closes clause 1, which qualifies the previous sentence (still, yet not sluggish); A is a legal subordinate shape rejected only by logic, as in 5aa171de and 21e58a83; B is the textbook placement; clause 2 opens with a “when” clause. Option set of f78997cf.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that explains it
items.passage: Recognized by UNESCO in 2020, the pantun is a Malay verse form whose four-line stanzas depend on a juxtaposition that often puzzles unfamiliar ______ opening couplet presenting an image from nature and a closing couplet expressing the poem’s actual message, the two connected largely through rhyme and suggestion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Recognized by UNESCO in 2020, the pantun is a Malay verse form whose four-line stanzas depend on a juxtaposition that often puzzles unfamiliar readers” is a complete clause. What follows (“an opening couplet presenting an image from nature and a closing couplet expressing the poem’s actual message ...”) is a noun phrase that explains what that juxtaposition is, so a colon correctly introduces it.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “An opening couplet presenting an image from nature and a closing couplet ...” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “an opening couplet presenting ... and a closing couplet expressing ...” is a noun phrase, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: Adding “it is” turns the explanation into a main clause, which then follows the first main clause with only a comma: a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Malay verse form). Band 6: the noun phrase after the colon is long and contains participles (“presenting”, “expressing”) and a trailing absolute phrase, so A and B can look like sentence breaks; C is e9aee0d8’s “extensive, it was a” recipe. No lone dash option (a dash would also be acceptable) and no comma-appositive option. Facts kept general (UNESCO inscription 2020; nature couplet, then message couplet).

band7.why: As targeted: colon before a long noun phrase with participles and an absolute; e9aee0d8 “it is” recipe; the announcing word sits a few words before the blank.

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive appositive (descriptor + name) followed by its verb
items.passage: The Jawahar Kala Kendra, a cultural center completed in Jaipur, India, in the early 1990s, is organized as a grid of nine squares, a configuration that Indian ______ adapted from the navagraha mandala, an ancient diagram representing the nine celestial bodies of Hindu cosmology.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Indian architect” is a title that comes directly before the name “Charles Correa” with no article, so the name is essential to identify who adapted the plan and is not set off with commas. Nor does any punctuation belong between the subject “Indian architect Charles Correa” and its verb “adapted.”

B.why_wrong: The commas treat “Charles Correa” as extra information, but without an article (“the”) before it, “Indian architect” is a title that needs the name to identify the person, so no commas are used.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “Correa” separates the subject “Indian architect Charles Correa” from its verb “adapted.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “Indian architect” from the name it introduces; the title and name together form the subject, so no comma belongs between them.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture, India). Band 7 (band7/boundaries.md section 5, S4_restrictive): article-less title + name inside a that-clause, followed directly by its verb, so the polite-looking comma pair (B, the hardest distractor) and the comma before the verb (C) both tempt; the passage already holds many commas around appositives (“a cultural center ...,” “Jaipur, India,” “the navagraha mandala, an ancient diagram ...”), which makes commas around the name look consistent. Facts kept to the well-known design: a nine-square plan Correa based on the navagraha mandala; completed in the early 1990s.

band7.why: Article-less title + name followed directly by its verb inside a that-clause, in a passage full of comma appositives; same shape and menu as 6d4b2e1e and 5aae2475. S4_restrictive is local at every band, so the verdict rests on that model match.

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive appositive (descriptor + name)
items.passage: Composed in the dialect of the cowhands of the pampas, El gaucho Martín Fierro (1872) follows a gaucho who is forcibly conscripted into military service on the frontier. The lengthy poem made Argentine ______ a household name among rural readers, many of whom purchased inexpensive editions at country stores.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Argentine journalist” is a descriptive title placed directly before the name “José Hernández,” with no article, so the name is essential and takes no punctuation. Together they form the object of “made,” which is followed by “a household name.”

A.why_wrong: The commas treat the name as an aside, but “Argentine journalist” without an article cannot stand alone as the object of “made”; the name is essential, so no commas are used.

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “The lengthy poem made Argentine journalist” is incomplete; the colon interrupts the object of “made.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “Argentine journalist” from the name that completes it.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Argentine gaucho poem). Band 6: plain title + name item (594b4a94, 80aa7690 menus); the name sits inside a “made X a household name” frame, so the reader must see that the object runs on past the name. Facts kept general (1872 poem in gaucho speech; hero conscripted for frontier service; widely sold to rural readers).

band7.why: As targeted: title + name as object of “made ... a household name”; 80aa7690 menu.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses; the second opens with a phrase that could attach to the first
items.passage: Archaeologists excavating Paquimé, a settlement that flourished in northern Mexico from about 1200 to 1450 CE, have uncovered adobe nesting boxes for scarlet macaws, birds native to forests far to the south. The city’s inhabitants likely bred the macaws for their brilliant ______ in the settlement’s plazas, dozens of the birds were ceremonially buried.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The city’s inhabitants likely bred the macaws for their brilliant plumage” and “in the settlement’s plazas, dozens of the birds were ceremonially buried” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the main clauses “The city’s inhabitants likely bred the macaws for their brilliant plumage” and “dozens of the birds were ceremonially buried”; “in the settlement’s plazas” opens the second clause and does not change that.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “in the settlement’s plazas” seems to tell where the macaws were bred, but “dozens of the birds were ceremonially buried” is a second main clause, so the comma after “plazas” joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses as long as these, a comma is used before it.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology, northern Mexico). S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6. Reviewer rebuilt it: the draft’s “, but” + plain subject is CB’s band 1 to 4 shape (155239cf, b6de636f); every band 5 and 6 comma_conj key is “, and” with a clause-2 opener that could attach to clause 1 (7ce4ee13 “New Mexico in 1928”, 59094d87). Here “in the settlement’s plazas” reads as where the macaws were bred until “dozens of the birds were ceremonially buried” arrives. Facts kept general (nesting boxes, macaws bred for plumage, macaw burials in plazas).

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials (band7/boundaries.md section 1). Draft read easier (“, but” + plain subject, CB band 1 to 4); rebuilt to “, and” + an attachable clause-2 opener, the band 6 shape of 7ce4ee13 and 59094d87.

fixes: rebuilt the sentence holding the blank: “south, but” + plain subject (CB band 1 to 4 shape) became “plumage, and” + an opener (“in the settlement’s plazas”) that can attach to clause 1, the band 5 to 6 shape of 7ce4ee13 and 59094d87; new options, explanation and why_wrong

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas; the deciding semicolon comes later
items.passage: Finnish artist Tove Jansson is best known for the Moomins, but her output extended considerably beyond them. She drew political cartoons, many of them ridiculing Hitler and ______ including two for a restaurant in Helsinki’s city hall; and illustrated books by other authors, such as a Swedish edition of The Hobbit.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence lists three things Jansson did, and each item contains its own comma (“political cartoons, many of them ...”; “murals, including ...”; “books by other authors, such as ...”), so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon before “and illustrated” shows. A semicolon therefore belongs after “Stalin,” and a comma after “murals” sets off the “including” phrase within the second item.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “Stalin” fails to separate the first two items with a semicolon, which is inconsistent with the semicolon that separates the second and third items.

C.why_wrong: The semicolon after “Stalin” is right, but a semicolon after “murals” cuts off “including two for a restaurant in Helsinki’s city hall,” which belongs to the second item and is not an item of its own.

D.why_wrong: The comma after “Stalin” fails to separate the items with a semicolon, and a colon after “murals” wrongly suggests that a list or explanation follows.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Finnish artist). Band 7 (band7/boundaries.md section 5, S5_series): blank in item 1, the revealing semicolon comes later (before “and illustrated”), and each option fixes a second slot inside item 2 (the comma before the “including” phrase), as in 9c3630b9 “leaves; man-made trash,”. No option omits the comma before “including” (that could read as acceptable). Facts kept to well-known ones: wartime cartoons mocking Hitler and Stalin; murals for a restaurant in Helsinki City Hall; illustrations for Swedish editions of Tolkien and Carroll.

band7.why: Blank in item 1, the deciding semicolon comes about 12 words later before “and illustrated”, and each option fixes a second slot inside item 2 (comma before “including”); menu of 9c3630b9.

fixes: “Swedish editions of The Hobbit” to “a Swedish edition of The Hobbit” (Jansson illustrated one Swedish edition, 1962)

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing noun phrase whose relative clause contains a finite verb
items.passage: Dracula ants of the species Mystrium camillae incapacitate prey by pressing their mandibles together until one slides past the other. In 2018, researchers filming the ants with high-speed cameras determined that this snap can reach 90 meters per ______ that, as far as the investigators could tell, makes it the fastest known motion of any animal appendage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2018, researchers filming the ants with high-speed cameras determined that this snap can reach 90 meters per second” is a complete clause. “A speed that, as far as the investigators could tell, makes it the fastest known motion of any animal appendage” is a noun phrase that comments on that figure; its verb “makes” belongs to the “that” clause, so the phrase is not a main clause and is joined to the sentence with a comma.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a speed that ... makes it the fastest known motion of any animal appendage” is a noun phrase; “makes” is the verb of the relative clause, not of a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “A speed that, as far as the investigators could tell, makes it the fastest known motion of any animal appendage” a separate sentence, but it lacks a main verb, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “a speed that ...” runs into “90 meters per second” with no boundary between the main clause and the supplementary phrase that describes it.

items.notes: Subject: science (insect biomechanics). Band 7 (band7/boundaries.md section 5, S2_trailing): a sentence appositive whose relative clause has a finite verb (“makes”) set 9 words past the blank behind an interrupter, so A and C look like they start a new clause (0b005ae2 “supposed, a finding that, if true, would”). No dash or colon option. Researchers left unnamed; facts kept general (2018 high-speed filming; snaps up to 90 m/s, reported as the fastest known animal appendage motion).

band7.why: Sentence appositive whose relative clause has a finite verb (“makes”) 9 words past the blank behind an interrupter, so semicolon and period look right; 0b005ae2 shape and menu.

items.subtype: No punctuation inside a compound object of two noun clauses joined by and
items.passage: More than 3,000 years ago, diviners at the Shang dynasty capital near present-day Anyang, China, heated cattle bones and turtle shells and interpreted the resulting cracks. Inscriptions on some of these oracle bones document what question the king had posed to his royal ______ and whether the predicted outcome subsequently occurred.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “document” has two coordinated objects joined by “and”: “what question the king had posed to his royal ancestors” and “whether the predicted outcome subsequently occurred.” Because there are only two coordinates and they are noun clauses rather than main clauses, no punctuation is needed between them.

A.why_wrong: A comma before “and” is used when “and” joins two main clauses, but here it joins the two objects of “document,” so the comma wrongly separates them.

B.why_wrong: A colon after “ancestors” would introduce an explanation, but “and whether ...” is the second half of a compound object, not an explanation of the first.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon joins main clauses, but “and whether the predicted outcome subsequently occurred” is a noun clause that completes the verb “document.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Shang divination, China). Planned as band 7, but S4_compound has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md section 1), so written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md: the first noun clause runs 11 words, so a comma before “and” feels natural (6ea8c23f shape). Facts kept general (heated bones and shells read for cracks; some inscriptions record whether the prediction came true).

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 officials (band7/boundaries.md section 1); a strong band 6 on the 6ea8c23f shape (two noun-clause objects, 11-word first clause, comma/colon/semicolon/none menu).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses; the second opens with a short phrase
items.passage: Tifinagh, an alphabet used to write Amazigh (Berber) languages, descends from an ancient script preserved in rock inscriptions throughout North Africa. In 2003, Morocco’s Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture adopted a standardized version of the ______ since then, the script has been incorporated into the curriculum of many of the country’s public schools.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2003, Morocco’s Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture adopted a standardized version of the alphabet” and “since then, the script has been incorporated into the curriculum ...” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; “since then” is a phrase that opens the second clause, not a conjunction.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is used before it.

items.notes: Subject: language (writing systems, North Africa). Medium: second clause opens with a short phrase (“since then,”), as in 2.2 and 2.5. Facts kept general (ancient Libyco-Berber roots in rock inscriptions; standardized in Morocco in 2003 and taught in schools).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: Sea pigs are plump, translucent sea cucumbers that wander across the deep-ocean floor on enlarged tube feet, consuming organic particles that settle into the sediment. They frequently congregate in herds whose members all face the same ______ facing into the current, the animals may be better positioned to detect the scent of food drifting toward them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “They frequently congregate in herds whose members all face the same direction” is a complete sentence. “By facing into the current” is an introductory phrase that leads into the next main clause (“the animals may be better positioned to detect ...”), so a period belongs after “direction.”

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “by facing into the current” seems to finish the first clause, but “the animals may be better positioned ...” is a second main clause, so two main clauses are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “by facing into the current” attaches to the first clause, and the comma before “the animals” then creates a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” would need a comma before it to join two main clauses of this length; as written, the sentences run together.

items.notes: Subject: science (deep-sea animals). Medium: a 5-word introductory phrase after the boundary (2.27 “adjustments. Prior to” menu, with “and” as the added word). Facts kept general (sea pigs walk on enlarged tube feet, gather in groups and tend to face into the current, perhaps to smell food).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Because ekiben, the boxed meals sold at railway stations throughout Japan, are typically designed to showcase local specialties, a station in a fishing town might offer ekiben filled with crab or squid, while one in an agricultural district might feature regional ______ each box a kind of edible souvenir of the journey.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A station in a fishing town might offer ekiben filled with crab or squid, while one in an agricultural district might feature regional beef” is the main clause of the sentence. “Making each box a kind of edible souvenir of the journey” is a participial phrase that comments on that whole idea, so a comma joins it to the sentence.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must be followed by a main clause, but “making each box a kind of edible souvenir” is a participial phrase.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Making each box a kind of edible souvenir of the journey” a separate sentence, but it has no subject or main verb.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “making each box ...” seems to describe “beef” rather than the whole idea of regional fillings; a comma is needed before this trailing phrase.

items.notes: Subject: social science (food culture and travel, Japan). Medium: trailing “-ing” phrase after a long sentence with an introductory “Because” clause and a “while” clause (2.4, 2.26 menus). Facts kept general.

items.subtype: Closing comma of an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Fogbows, faint arcs of light that form when sunlight passes through the minuscule droplets of ______ almost white, since droplets that small cause the colors of sunlight to overlap instead of separating into distinct bands.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “faint arcs of light that form when sunlight passes through the minuscule droplets of fog” describes “Fogbows” and is opened by a comma after “Fogbows.” A second comma must close it, so that the subject “Fogbows” connects cleanly to its verb, “look.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the supplementary phrase opened by the comma after “Fogbows” is never closed off from the verb “look.”

B.why_wrong: The phrase was opened with a comma, so it must be closed with a comma, not a dash.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “Fogbows” from its verb “look,” leaving neither side a complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (atmospheric optics). Medium: partner comma 15 words before the blank, right after the subject (2.1 shape). Facts kept general (fogbows look nearly white because fog droplets are small).

fixes: “to overlap rather than separating them” to “to overlap instead of separating” (“rather than” after an infinitive mixed verb forms)

items.subtype: Closing dash of a dash pair that holds an inner comma
items.passage: For more than six centuries, Ethiopia’s emperors invoked a single text to legitimize their claim to the throne. The Kebra Nagast (“Glory of the Kings”)—compiled in the fourteenth century in Ge’ez, the classical liturgical language of ______ the dynasty’s descent from King Solomon of Israel and the Queen of Sheba.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The supplementary element “compiled in the fourteenth century in Ge’ez, the classical liturgical language of Ethiopia” is opened with a dash after the title, so a second dash must close it before the verb “traces.”

A.why_wrong: The comma closes only the inner phrase “the classical liturgical language of Ethiopia”; the element that was opened with a dash still needs a closing dash.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon would cut the subject “The Kebra Nagast” off from its verb “traces,” and neither side would be a main clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the supplementary element opened by the dash runs straight into the main verb “traces.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Ethiopian text in Ge’ez). Medium: the dash opens 13 words before the blank, and an inner comma (“Ge’ez, the classical liturgical language ...”) makes the comma option look right (2.13 menu). Facts kept general (compiled in the fourteenth century in Ge’ez; traces the dynasty to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba; long used to support the emperors’ claim).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that specifies it
items.passage: Drawn around 1150 BCE by the scribe Amennakhte, the Turin Papyrus Map depicts a section of Egypt’s Wadi Hammamat, a desert valley whose quarries supplied stone for royal statues. The map incorporates a feature that was exceptionally rare in ancient ______ use of color to indicate which varieties of rock appear in different parts of the valley.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The map incorporates a feature that was exceptionally rare in ancient cartography” is a complete clause, and “the use of color to indicate which varieties of rock appear in different parts of the valley” is a noun phrase that specifies that feature. A colon correctly introduces it.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “the use of color to indicate ...” is a noun phrase, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “The use of color to indicate which varieties of rock appear ...” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the noun phrase “the use of color ...” runs into the clause with nothing to mark that it specifies “a feature.”

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient Egyptian map). Medium: complete clause ending in an announcing noun (“a feature”), then a noun phrase with a “which” clause (2.15 shape; options without a comma-appositive twin and without a dash). Facts kept general (scribe Amennakhte, about 1150 BCE; Wadi Hammamat quarries; colored areas marking rock types).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Measuring more than 100 meters in diameter, Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park is the largest hot spring in the United States. The brilliant bands of orange, yellow, and green that encircle its deep-blue center are produced ______ dense mats of heat-tolerant microorganisms, each adapted to a particular range of water temperatures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “By” is a preposition, and “dense mats of heat-tolerant microorganisms” is its object. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: The dash separates the preposition “by” from its object “dense mats of heat-tolerant microorganisms” for no reason.

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “The brilliant bands ... are produced by” is not complete without its object.

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “by” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: science (geothermal microbiology). Easy: passive “by” and its object (1.21 menu). Facts kept general.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Cumbia, a style of music and dance that originated on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, spread across Latin America during the twentieth century. In the late 1960s, musicians in Peru began to ______ rhythms with electric guitars and Andean melodies, creating a distinctive regional sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In this sentence, “its rhythms” is the object of the verb “combine.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “musicians in Peru began to combine” needs its object to be complete.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the verb “combine” from its object “its rhythms.”

D.why_wrong: The dash separates the verb “combine” from its object for no reason.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Latin American music). Easy: verb and object (1.15 menu). Facts kept general (cumbia from Colombia’s Caribbean coast; Peruvian groups of the late 1960s adding electric guitars and Andean melodies).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Since 1956, the British government has offered savers Premium Bonds, an investment that functions somewhat like a lottery. Bondholders don’t receive ______ each bond is automatically entered into a monthly prize draw with tax-free rewards ranging from modest sums to one million pounds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Bondholders don’t receive interest” and “each bond is automatically entered into a monthly prize draw ...” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “but” here; it separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses.

items.notes: Subject: social science (personal finance, UK). Easy: two clauses joined by “, but” (1.27, 1.31 menus). Facts kept general (Premium Bonds since 1956; no interest; monthly tax-free prize draw with a top prize of one million pounds).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Light pillars are bright vertical columns that sometimes appear above streetlights when temperatures drop far below freezing. Because they form only when flat, hexagonal ice crystals float in the air near the ______ pillars are seen most often in regions with especially harsh winters, such as Alaska and northern Canada.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Because they form only when flat, hexagonal ice crystals float in the air near the ground” is an introductory dependent clause, and “light pillars are seen most often ...” is the main clause. A comma correctly separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Because they form only when ...” is a dependent clause.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “Because they form only when flat, hexagonal ice crystals float in the air near the ground” as a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Adding “and” pulls “light pillars are seen ...” into the “Because” clause, so the sentence never reaches a main clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (atmospheric optics). Easy: “Because” clause before the subject (1.6, 1.8 menus). Facts kept general.

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement word order and a period
items.passage: The Darvaza gas crater in Turkmenistan’s Karakum Desert is a pit about 70 meters wide that has been burning for decades. According to a widely repeated story, geologists deliberately set the gas on fire in 1971, but that account has never been confirmed, and researchers remain uncertain about exactly when ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “When the fire was started” is an embedded question: it is part of a statement (“researchers remain uncertain about exactly when ...”), not a question of its own. It therefore uses statement word order and ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: The sentence is a statement about what researchers don’t know, so it takes neither question word order (“was the fire started”) nor a question mark.

C.why_wrong: The period is right, but an embedded question keeps statement word order (“the fire was started”), not question order.

D.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology, Central Asia). Easy: embedded question at the end of the passage (1.7, 1.24). Facts kept general (crater about 70 m wide; the 1971 ignition story is unconfirmed).

items.subtype: Commas between items in a simple series
items.passage: Sijo, a form of Korean poetry that dates back at least to the fourteenth century, was traditionally sung rather than simply read aloud. Its three lines, each containing about fourteen to sixteen syllables, often explore themes such as ______ loyalty, and the beauty of the changing seasons.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Love,” “loyalty,” and “the beauty of the changing seasons” are three items in a simple series. A comma separates the first item from the second.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon is used between series items only when the items contain commas; these items do not.

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate two items in a list.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “love” and “loyalty” run together instead of reading as separate items.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Korean verse form). Easy: three-item list, blank after item 1 (1.3 menu). Facts kept general.

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that-clause
items.passage: Japanese architect Kenzo Tange was known for blending modern engineering with forms from traditional Japanese buildings. For the 1964 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, he designed the Yoyogi National Gymnasium, a swimming ______ is still admired for its sweeping roof, which is suspended from steel cables strung between two concrete masts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That is still admired for its sweeping roof” is an integrated (restrictive) relative clause that gives essential information about “a swimming arena.” The relative pronoun “that” is needed to link the verb “is still admired” to that noun, and no comma separates the noun from a restrictive clause.

A.why_wrong: With only a comma and no “that,” the verb phrase “is still admired ...” has no subject of its own and cannot attach to “a swimming arena” or to the rest of the sentence.

B.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb phrase “is still admired ...” has no subject and cannot attach to “a swimming arena.”

C.why_wrong: A comma does not go before “that” when it introduces a restrictive clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture, Japan). Easy: restrictive that-clause after a noun in an appositive (1.29 menu: “company,” / “company that” / “company” / “company, that”). Facts kept general (Tange blended modern engineering with traditional forms; Yoyogi gymnasium for the 1964 Olympics, its roof hung from cables between two concrete masts).
